How Sudoku works, and your first move
Fill the grid so that every row, every column and every 3×3 box contains each number from 1 to 9 exactly once.\n\nThe grid has 9 rows, 9 columns and 9 boxes. Together we call them houses.

Some numbers are given at the start and never change. Every puzzle in this app has exactly one solution, and you can always reach it by logic alone.\n\nThe lessons show you the techniques to find the next number.
The easiest move: when a row, column or box has only one empty cell left, it gets the one number that is still missing.\n\nNext you\'ll see an example, then it\'s your turn.
Find the only place a number can go
Pick a number and a box. For each empty cell of the box, check if the number already appears in that cell\'s row or column. If it does, the number can\'t go there.

If just one cell remains, the number must go there. This is called a hidden single, because the cell might have other options – but the number has nowhere else to go.\n\nThe same works for rows and columns.
Start with numbers that already appear often on the board. They rule out the most cells, so hidden singles are easiest to spot with them.\n\nTap a number on the board to highlight all of its copies.
Find the only number a cell can hold
Now turn it around: pick an empty cell and collect every number that already appears in its row, its column and its box.
If eight different numbers are already taken, the ninth is the only one that fits. This is called a naked single.\n\nLook for cells whose row, column and box are already quite full.
Use notes to rule numbers out

Harder puzzles need notes. The candidates of a cell are all numbers that could still go there. Write them as small numbers into the cell.\n\nIn the game, turn on Notes mode to do this. In these exercises the candidates are already filled in.
If two cells in the same house have exactly the same two candidates – say 3 and 7 – then these two cells take the 3 and the 7, in some order.
So no other cell in that house can be a 3 or a 7. Remove both numbers from the candidates of all other cells in the house.\n\nTo remove a candidate, select the cell and tap the number.
When a box points along a line
Look at one number inside a box. If all of its candidates in that box lie in the same row, the number has to go in that row – somewhere inside this box.\n\nThe same goes for columns.
Because the box will use the number in that row, no other cell of the row can have it. Remove the number from the cells of the row that are outside the box.
Two numbers that claim two cells
Look at two numbers in one house. If both can only go in the same two cells, those cells are reserved for them – one gets each number.
So these two cells can\'t hold anything else. Remove all other candidates from them.\n\nHidden pairs are harder to see than naked pairs, because the extra candidates hide them.
